newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Thai PTT reviews overseas oil plans on baht fall.
newsitem.headline: Thai PTT reviews overseas oil plans on baht fall.

text.p: State-owned Petroleum Authority of Thailand's (PTT) international arm aims to streamline its overseas downstream investments and cut costs due to the baht's sharp fall, a senior executive said on Thursday. The sharp drop has prompted PTT International to take a second look at an earlier budget review by focusing on fewer countries and to extend the completion period for overseas projects, Nuttachat Charuchinda, senior vice president for marketing and joint ventures told Reuters by telephone.

"We have already made some reviews but since there is also some effect from the baht devaluation, we have to review that again and put that into the picture. We will get a clearer picture next month," he said from Bangkok.
"We want to tighten our belts too, so we are reviewing all the plans and looking at them on a project-by-project basis to set our priorities," he said.
Late in 1995, PTT International announced plans to invest 13 billion baht over the next five years to transform itself into a regional energy company.
Last Wednesday, the Thai government allowed the baht to float, replacing a system whch had pegged the baht to a basket of currencies dominated by the dollar.
This triggered an immediate 20 percent plunge in value of the baht which was last quoted on the offshore market at 29.03/29.13 per dollar.
The baht slump has also turned the 13 billion baht budget into a U.S. dollar equivalent of 450 million from 514 million when it was set last year.
Nuttachat said he was "a bit" surprised by the extent of the fall.
Another source said PTT International had expected the devaluation to be limited to five percent.
Nuttachat said PTT International will focus on projects in China, the Philippines and will venture into Bangladesh.
But India and Sri Lanka would not be given priority while its Indochina ventures would also be under review, he said.
India had initially been the company's focus in South Asia, with plans to penetrate the liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) sector and to start a network of petrol stations.
Nuttachat now said "India is too crowded", referring to the number of oil firms that have already made inroads into the country.
PTT International plans to invest six-billion baht in the Philippines to build 265 service stations by 2006, with 144 earlier projected to start in five years.
It also has a joint-venture with the Coastal Aruba Refining Co N.V. to co-lease oil supply depots at Subic Bay and the former Clark Air Base.
Another PTT source said the company might reduce the number of petrol stations in the Philippines in view of the Baht fall.
Nuttachat said while this was being considered, the likely scenario was that the targetted number might be retained but the period to build them would be extended by one or two years.
"We may suspend some investments but in the long term our target will stay the same," he said.
He however said that the effects of the lower baht was not all bad because the company gains when it exports LPG to China and Vietnam in U.S. dollars.

PTT International is in a $90 million joint venture to build a 50,000-tonne LPG depot in the southeastern Chinese city of Shantuo, which when completed in 1999 will store imported LPG from the Middle East.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65-870 3084)
